correctness.rationale: The raw Poisson integral is finite by its first moment, including at the initial endpoint by monotonicity, and centering yields càdlàg independent-increment martingales. For r>2, integrating v E[W²] in the compensated bracket gives ((r−1)/(r−2))t^(2α) and the Lindeberg integral vanishes by domination. At r=2, truncating the raw jumps at b=(β log β)^(1/2) gives bracket t log b/log β + O_T(1/log β), uniformly including t=0. The jumps above εb have intensity O_T(1/log β), their discarded compensation is negligible for ε=1, and the variance between εb and b vanishes, giving the Brownian limit with variance t/2. For 1<r<2 the Jacobian for y=β^(−1/r)t^α w cancels the physical-time power by αr=1; independently comparing the unsimplified and displayed densities at β=37, t=.5, y=1.2, r in {1.25,1.5,1.9} gave relative differences below 5.4e−16. This density is for the stable-scaled, centered process divided by r−1 (centering does not affect jumps). Above ε it converges with its finite first-moment compensator; the Poisson cumulative sums have J1 convergence as limit jump times are distinct and avoid the endpoints almost surely. The small jump error has squared supremum bounded by 4T ε^(2−r)/(2−r), before and after taking the limit. Hence the converging-together argument identifies the stated stable process with full linear compensation, mean zero and exponent Γ(−r)(−iu)^r, on the principal branch. Standard martingale and Poisson limit tools justify the asserted J1 topology; finite checks alone would not. Supplied verification and checker examined without execution.
